title: Monday, 6:00 a.m.: who connects first
note: Fictional unit and patients. Thresholds for potassium, weight gain, pressure and glucose are your unit’s; the attending nephrologist sets the plan.
intro:
You are the charge nurse on Monday morning, after the two-day gap. Three stations will be ready at 06:15. Four patients are in the waiting area:

  • Mr. Ramon Cruz, 71, heart failure: 3.8 kg above his dry weight of 58 kg, pressure 172/96. He slept sitting up on Saturday night.
  • Mr. Jun Dizon, 45: missed Friday’s session (no transport). He says his legs feel heavy and weak.
  • Mrs. Elena Santos, 59, on insulin: weight and pressure as usual.
  • Mrs. Lourdes Navarro, 64: comfortable, weight gain 1.9 kg.

n1.prompt: Which findings go in the Now lane, for a physician before connection?

choices.text: Mr. Cruz’s orthopnea and Mr. Dizon’s missed session with leg weakness.
choices.feedback: New orthopnea is a Now finding. So is a patient who missed Friday and now has weakness after the long gap: his potassium may be high, and weakness can be a sign of it. Both get a physician before connection.

choices.text: Mr. Cruz only. Mr. Dizon simply needs the session he missed, so connect him first and tell the physician during it.
choices.feedback: Connecting him first is reasonable, but not before a physician knows. Weakness after a missed session is a Now finding: the physician may want a potassium and an ECG (electrocardiogram) first, and a plan for what to do if they are abnormal.
choices.then: The staff nurse starts preparing Mr. Dizon’s station. You stop and phone the physician on duty, Dr. Aquino, before the needles go in.

choices.text: None of them yet. Weigh everyone, take full vital signs, and collect the laboratory results before calling anyone, so the physician gets one complete report.
choices.feedback: A complete report is good, but the lanes are about speed. Orthopnea and possible hyperkalemia should not wait for the rest of the floor. Call with what you have and add the rest.
choices.then: Twenty minutes pass. Mr. Cruz is now breathing faster in his chair. You call Dr. Aquino.

n2.scene: Dr. Aquino asks for Mr. Dizon to get a potassium and an ECG now and to connect first; he will review both. The staff nurse’s plan for Mr. Cruz is to remove the full 3.8 liters in four hours.
n2.prompt: What do you do about Mr. Cruz’s plan?

choices.text: Work out the rate (about 16 mL/kg/h) and ask Dr. Aquino before connection.
choices.feedback: 3,800 mL ÷ 4 h ÷ 58 kg is about 16 mL/kg/h. High rates are associated with more deaths and with heart-muscle stunning in observational studies. Setting the plan is the physician’s job; noticing the number and asking before connection is yours.
choices.then: Dr. Aquino extends the session and lowers the hourly goal, and asks for a review of Mr. Cruz’s dry weight this week.

choices.text: Let the staff nurse lower the goal to 3 liters herself, since a smaller target is always safer for a heart failure patient.
choices.feedback: Leaving fluid on a man who is already orthopneic is not automatically safer, and changing the goal is not a nursing decision. Show the physician the rate and let him set the plan.
choices.then: You call Dr. Aquino instead; he extends the session and lowers the hourly goal.

choices.text: Run the plan as written; he is overloaded and needs every liter off today.
choices.feedback: Needing the fluid off does not mean taking it off fast. At about 16 mL/kg/h, a 71-year-old with heart failure is at real risk of a pressure fall mid-session.
choices.then: At hour 2 his pressure falls to 88/50 and fluid removal is stopped. Dr. Aquino rewrites the plan with a longer session.

n3.scene: Mr. Dizon is connected first; his potassium is 6.6 mmol/L and Dr. Aquino is reviewing the ECG. When you ask Mrs. Santos your two questions, she says she took her usual insulin at 5:00 but did not eat because she felt rushed.

choices.text: Check her glucose now, give her food per protocol, and tell the physician.
choices.feedback: Glucose falls during dialysis, lowest around the second hour. Insulin without breakfast is the setup for a low sugar in the chair. Check it, feed her, and make it a Today finding for the physician.
choices.then: Her glucose is 96 mg/dL. She eats a sandwich before connection, and the nurse checks again at hour 2.

choices.text: Connect her on time and check her glucose at hour 2, when the fall during dialysis is usually lowest.
choices.feedback: Hour 2 is the right time to recheck, but she needs a reading and food before connection too. Insulin with no breakfast means her glucose may already be low.
choices.then: At hour 2 she is sweaty; her glucose is 58 mg/dL and is treated by protocol.

choices.text: Remind her firmly that she must always eat after taking insulin, and add a note for the dietitian to see her this week.
choices.feedback: Teaching matters, but it does not protect her today. She has insulin on board and no food: check her glucose and feed her before connection.
choices.then: At hour 2 she is sweaty; her glucose is 58 mg/dL and is treated by protocol.

n4.scene: Going through the weekend laboratory reports, you find Mrs. Navarro’s Friday potassium: 6.3 mmol/L, reported Saturday. There is no note that anyone called a physician. She looks well and is next in line.
n4.prompt: Who owns this result now, and what do you do?

choices.text: You do. Call Dr. Aquino before connection, record the decision, and name who acts next.
choices.feedback: A critical result is closed only when it is received, told, decided, recorded and owned. This one broke at the second link. If a result has no named owner, it belongs to the charge nurse until it does.
choices.then: Dr. Aquino orders a repeat potassium before connection and writes the plan.

choices.text: Connect her; dialysis treats the potassium anyway. Then ask the weekend nurse on Wednesday why the result was never called in.
choices.feedback: Dialysis may well be the treatment, but the physician has to decide that, and the result still needs closing today. Finding out who missed it can wait; closing the loop cannot.
choices.then: You call Dr. Aquino before connection; he orders a repeat potassium.

choices.text: Leave it for the physician’s rounds; she looks well.
choices.feedback: Looking well does not rule out a dangerous potassium. Without a named owner, this result could slip again.
choices.then: You think again and call Dr. Aquino; he orders a repeat potassium before connection.

n5.scene: Mr. Cruz’s wife stops you at the door. He fell at home on Saturday night getting up to the bathroom. He says he is fine and has no pain.
n5.prompt: Which lane, and what do you do?

choices.text: Today: check him for injury, tell the physician this session, and help him stand afterward.
choices.feedback: A fall since the last session is a Today finding. Look for injury now and tell the physician during the session. Falls are common in older patients on dialysis, and he will be at his lowest pressure when he stands up after treatment.

choices.text: Now: disconnect him and send him for X-rays before the session continues, because a fall in a man his age can hide a fracture.
choices.feedback: He has no pain and no visible injury, and he needs the session. Check him and tell the physician, who decides whether he needs imaging.

choices.text: This month: add it to his care-plan review.
choices.feedback: A recent fall needs attention today: an injury check, the physician told, and help with standing after the session.

end.text: All four patients are on. Mr. Dizon’s potassium is being removed under Dr. Aquino’s plan, Mr. Cruz is on a longer session, Mrs. Santos has eaten, and Mrs. Navarro’s result has an owner. You write the morning’s calls in the charge log and ask for the weekend-result process to be on Wednesday’s staff meeting agenda.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Monday is the riskiest morning. The patient who missed Friday is the riskiest patient of the week.
  • Sort by speed: Now (physician before connection), Today (during the session), This month.
  • Work out the fluid-removal rate and ask before connection when it is high.
  • Ask every patient on insulin or a sulfonylurea what they took and what they ate.
  • A result with no owner is yours until someone else owns it.

See Now, Today, This month, Fluid and the speed of removal and Closing the loop.
